title: Mean Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Mean Calculator: Arithmetic mean (average) of a list of numbers. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and answers to common questions.
content:
The [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Arithmetic mean (average) of a list of numbers. Enter your numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find the arithmetic mean — the average — of a list of numbers: add them all up and divide by how many there are. It is the single number most people mean when they say “average”, and it is how averages are reported for grades, measurements, survey scores and sports statistics. The calculator also shows the sum, the count and the smallest and largest values, so you can see whether one extreme value is pulling the average away from the middle of the list.

## How to use the Mean Calculator

Start by typing or pasting your numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Paste or type your numbers, separated by commas, spaces or new lines.
2. Read the mean — the sum, count, smallest and largest values are shown too.
3. Add or remove numbers to see how the average moves.

## Formula

Mean = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) ÷ n, where n is how many numbers there are. For example, the mean of 4, 8 and 15 is (4 + 8 + 15) ÷ 3 = 9.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The mean of 4, 8, 15, 16, 23 and 42 is 18: the numbers add up to 108 and there are 6 of them, so 108 ÷ 6 = 18. Try the same figures in the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines): 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42), the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) returns Mean (average): 18, Sum: 108, Count: 6, Smallest: 4, Largest: 42. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## When the mean misleads

The mean is sensitive to extreme values. A list like 2, 3, 4, 5, 100 has a mean of 22.8, even though four of the five numbers are under 6. When a few very large or very small values are present, the median (the middle value) is often a fairer summary — try the median calculator on the same list and compare.

## Mean, median and mode together

The three averages answer different questions. The mean is the balance point of the data, the median is the middle value, and the mode is the most common value. When all three are close together, the data is roughly symmetric; when they differ a lot, the data is skewed. Reporting all three gives a much better picture than any one alone.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Separate numbers with commas, spaces or new lines — any of them works.
- If one huge value is dragging the mean away, check the median too.
- The mean of a single number is that number itself.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the mean?

The arithmetic mean is the sum of a list of numbers divided by how many numbers there are. It is the usual meaning of “average”. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do you calculate the mean?

Add up all the numbers, then divide by the count. For 4, 8 and 15: (4 + 8 + 15) ÷ 3 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between the mean and the median?

The mean is the total divided by the count; the median is the middle value when the numbers are sorted. The median ignores extreme values, so it is steadier when the data has outliers. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Can the mean be a decimal?

Yes — the mean is often a decimal even when every input is a whole number, for example the mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mean Calculator](/mean-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
